targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Definition of the problem: given two non‑decreasing integer arrays of size m and n, find the median of the combined sorted array in O(log (m+n)) time.
targets.why_assessed: Checks that students can precisely state the problem constraints and expected output.
plausible_misconceptions: Confusing median with mean
Assuming arrays must be of equal length

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Derivation of the binary‑search partition strategy that guarantees left‑side elements ≤ right‑side elements across both arrays.
targets.why_assessed: Ensures students grasp why the partition method yields the correct median and why logarithmic time is achievable.
plausible_misconceptions: Believing the algorithm relies on merging the arrays
Thinking the partition must be exactly at half the total length

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Implementation details: use of integer division to compute partition indices, handling of edge values with +/-∞ sentinel, and swapping arrays to ensure binary search on the shorter array.
targets.why_assessed: Tests ability to read and explain each line of a reference implementation.
plausible_misconceptions: Misinterpreting the sentinel values as actual data
Overlooking the array‑swap precondition

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Step‑by‑step execution on concrete inputs, e.g., A=[1,3,8], B=[7,9,10,11]; compute partitions and derive median 8.
targets.why_assessed: Validates tracing ability and correct calculation of the median from intermediate partition values.
plausible_misconceptions: Using the wrong partition index for one array
Averaging the wrong two numbers when total length is even

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Common bugs: off‑by‑one in partition calculation, failure to update low/high correctly, missing handling of empty array.
targets.why_assessed: Encourages students to locate and fix logical errors in a faulty implementation.
plausible_misconceptions: Assuming the algorithm never needs to check for empty arrays
Thinking that decreasing high by 1 always moves the partition left

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Handling of extreme cases: one array empty, arrays of size 1, total length odd vs even, and maximum integer values.
targets.why_assessed: Ensures robustness by testing student reasoning on edge conditions.
plausible_misconceptions: Returning the first element of the non‑empty array without checking parity
Using INT_MAX/INT_MIN incorrectly as sentinels

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Effect of altering input sizes, e.g., doubling one array length, and how the partition indices adapt without changing algorithmic complexity.
targets.why_assessed: Tests adaptability of the method when problem parameters vary.
plausible_misconceptions: Assuming time complexity changes with uneven size growth
Believing the partition formula must be recomputed from scratch

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Proof that the algorithm runs in O(log min(m,n)) time and O(1) extra space, including worst‑case scenario analysis.
targets.why_assessed: Confirms mastery of asymptotic reasoning specific to this algorithm.
plausible_misconceptions: Confusing O(log (m+n)) with O(log m + log n)
Neglecting the constant‑space claim

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Contrast between the binary‑search partition method and the naïve merge‑then‑pick approach, highlighting trade‑offs in time and space.
targets.why_assessed: Encourages evaluation of algorithmic design choices.
plausible_misconceptions: Thinking both methods have identical space usage
Assuming merge approach can be made O(log n) without extra data structures

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Applying the median‑of‑two‑sorted‑arrays routine to real‑world scenarios such as finding the median salary from two departmental reports without merging full datasets.
targets.why_assessed: Demonstrates transfer of the algorithm to a realistic problem domain.
plausible_misconceptions: Assuming the algorithm can handle unsorted input
Overlooking privacy concerns when merging data

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays

targets.why_assessed: Checks that students grasp the fundamental problem statement and key invariants before applying any algorithm.
plausible_misconceptions: Confusing median with average
Assuming arrays must be of equal length

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Derivation of the binary search partition condition (max left ≤ min right) and why O(log min(m,n)) time is achievable.
targets.why_assessed: Ensures students can justify the design choices behind the logarithmic solution rather than memorizing steps.
plausible_misconceptions: Believing linear merge is optimal
Misunderstanding why the smaller array is chosen for binary search

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Explanation of a reference implementation in C++/Java/Python, focusing on index calculations, sentinel handling, and loop termination conditions.
targets.why_assessed: Tests ability to read and map code constructs to the algorithmic idea, a prerequisite for debugging and adaptation.
plausible_misconceptions: Treating i and j as array lengths instead of partition indices
Ignoring integer division rounding effects

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Step‑by‑step execution trace on two concrete arrays, including intermediate partition values and final median computation.
targets.why_assessed: Requires students to simulate the algorithm mentally, reinforcing understanding of control flow and data movement.
plausible_misconceptions: Predicting median of merged array without considering partition logic
Off‑by‑one errors in index selection

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Common bugs such as out‑of‑range access when i=0 or i=m, incorrect sentinel values, and failure to update low/high correctly.
targets.why_assessed: Develops diagnostic skills by having students locate and fix realistic implementation errors.
plausible_misconceptions: Assuming array bounds are automatically protected
Thinking that swapping low/high fixes all errors

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Handling of empty arrays, arrays of length 1, and extreme value extremes (INT_MAX/INT_MIN) as partition boundaries.
targets.why_assessed: Ensures robustness by testing understanding of edge conditions that often cause runtime failures.
plausible_misconceptions: Neglecting sentinel initialization
Assuming both arrays must contain at least two elements

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Effect of swapping the role of the two input arrays, changing array sizes, and modifying the target rank (e.g., kth smallest instead of median).
targets.why_assessed: Promotes flexibility by asking students to adapt the algorithm to altered parameters while preserving correctness.
plausible_misconceptions: Thinking the algorithm only works for exact median
Forgetting to recompute partition formulas after swapping

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Derivation of O(log min(m,n)) time and O(1) extra space, and comparison with O(m+n) merge approach.
targets.why_assessed: Validates ability to reason about asymptotic performance and space trade‑offs, crucial for algorithm selection.
plausible_misconceptions: Assuming binary search adds linear overhead
Confusing worst‑case with average‑case

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Contrast between the binary‑search partition method and the classic merge‑then‑pick approach, highlighting when each is preferable.
targets.why_assessed: Encourages higher‑order evaluation of algorithmic design choices in different contexts.
plausible_misconceptions: Believing one method is universally superior

targets.concept_name: DAA Median of Two Sorted Arrays
targets.what_taught: Specific traps such as treating median index as (m+n)/2 without floor/ceil adjustment for odd total length.
targets.why_assessed: Directly addresses a known student misconception to prevent systematic errors.
plausible_misconceptions: Using integer division that truncates incorrectly
Assuming median index is always integer without handling parity
